name: Interruptions
explanation: Users should be able to postpone or turn off interruptions they didn't ask for, such as pop-up notifications, alerts, or session-refresh prompts. This doesn't ban interruptions outright. It requires giving the user control over when they happen. That way, a user isn't forced to break concentration or lose their place in a task the moment content decides to interrupt them. The only exception is genuine emergencies, where the interruption needs to happen right away regardless of user preference.
whoItAffects: People with cognitive or attention-related disabilities can lose track of what they were doing when an unexpected interruption breaks their focus. They may need to restart a multi-step task mentally. Screen reader users can have an interruption announced right in the middle of content they're already listening to. This forces them to reorient and often re-find their place. Giving users a way to suppress or postpone non-emergency interruptions lets them finish what they're doing first.
howToTest: Use the site for a while and note any content that interrupts you without you asking for it: pop-ups, banners, session-timeout prompts, "new content available" notices. For each one, check whether there's a way to dismiss it and prevent it recurring, or postpone it until you choose to deal with it. If an interruption keeps recurring with no way to suppress it, and it isn't a genuine emergency notice, this fails.

check.question: A news site shows a "Breaking news" modal that interrupts reading every few minutes for non-urgent story updates, with no setting to turn it off or postpone it. Does this pass SC 2.2.4 Interruptions?
choices: Yes, because breaking news is inherently time-sensitive content
No, because the interruption isn't a genuine emergency and the user has no way to postpone or suppress it
Yes, because modals are a standard way to draw attention to updates
It depends only on how long each modal stays on screen
